Jack Prescott@JackPrescottX
11:20 SGT quoteInvesting
$ABCL I asked @bot to make a chart of AbCellera’s open market insider buys over the years.

I see 6 instances over the past four years where Carl dropped between about $700k-$1M on shares. It almost seems like it’s scheduled - like he’s taking his salary + bonus and dumping it into the stock or something. Whatever the reason is, I’ll take it. You love to see insider buying.

It’s interesting to see all the buying during 2022. Management was bullish, which makes sense since they were profitable with the COVID drugs at that time. Stock was around the same price that it is today.

Also, those two buys in Q3’24 and Q1’25… the stock was close to $2.00. It was psychologically tough as a shareholder. There was hardly any news other than knowing 575 and 635 would be entering the clinic soon and that the GMP facility was being finished up. Abbvie collab announcement was exciting but did nothing for the stock. Low volume. Management was always tight lipped on calls. Those insider buys helped keep shareholders sane.

Also notice there has only been one instance of insider selling since going public, and it was all in a single quarter after the IPO lockup. They got the bag, which they deserved. Zero selling since - only buying.

Something to consider though is how much they made during that sale. For example, Carl sold nearly $150M in stock. So when he drops $1M on some shares, it’s a negligible amount of his net worth. It does add up over time though. I think he’s bought over $20M in shares since.

Michael Hayden’s purchase in Q3 seems most notable. Don’t know his net worth but I’d say that $1M in purchases were probably the most noteworthy out of all relative to his net worth. Was right after the ph2 readouts. Love to see booth buying, too.

Carl must now own over 21% of the whole company. That’s a founder with real skin in the game.

$NBIS $MU $SNDK $LITE $COHR $BE

THIS IS THE UNCOMFORTABLE MOMENT WHEN YOU MUST MAKE A DECISION.

This is the winter when you get fit for the summer.

This is the pain before the gains.

This is as close to a bottom as you're going to get, when bad news no longer takes us lower.

The reality is that we most likely won't get a V-shaped recovery for semis, not because the AI trade is dead, but because hedge funds won't rotate heavily into these names until early next year.

Institutional investors are accumulating heavily here while retail is panic selling.

I'm telling you this because I don't want to see you chasing next year after the rally has already happened.

YOU DON'T GO TO THE GYM ONLY IN THE SUMMER TO GET FIT.

You grind all year so you reach the summer already fit.

I was telling myself and my own subscribers how horrible September felt, all the macro was sounding the alarms and the result was an October when the AI trade felt like -50%.

I'm telling you this now: this is the uncomfortable moment when you must accept that it's going to be a volatile ride. Look for stocks that are starting to outperform and aren't going back to last Thursday's prices, the ones with signed contracts, accelerating revenue and a peak that hasn't been reached yet.

My best estimate is that before the second half of 2027, we'll be much higher than we are today.

The whole semi index is STILL trading below July's low.

$NVDA is trading at 165
$NBIS is trading at 130
$BE is trading at 205
$SNDK is trading at 950
$MU is trading at 850
$LITE is trading at 630

$COHR is trading at 236

I'll quote this tweet, not delete it, and own the result.

I'm much more afraid of missing this new chance in the AI trade than of watching from the sidelines.

Demand for compute is higher, GPU rental prices are higher, capex will be raised once the productivity gains become obvious, and 2027 will be the year corporations adopt AI en masse and embed it into their workflows.

This trade will become crowded again, but until then, it's one of the best risk-reward investments you can make right now.

Fortune favors the bold, so I'll do exactly that.

In this rapid-fire round of Elections with TOI, Meghna puts Indrajeet Rai and Kunal Varma on the spot with questions about Congress's electoral challenges, the BJP's prospects in Uttar Pradesh, Punjab's political equation and the 2029 Lok Sabha elections.

The discussion also explores the possible political consequences of a BJP defeat in UP, including Indrajeet Rai's striking suggestion that India could see elections before 2029.

Sorry, but anyone complaining about Nvidia's board is an absolute S-Tier idiot.

1. Jensen resigned. Don't you think Jensen/the board would've drawn this out for longer if the walls weren't closing in on him?

2. Jensen having TWO undisclosed relationships with subordinates goes against Nvidia's Code of Conduct.

A company's Code of Conduct applies to ALL employees, including the Founder and CEO.
Does holding the title of CEO allow you to wield your power and circumvent the Code of Conduct?

Given Jensen's role, this question becomes a lot more philosophical and blurry.

But rules are rules, and I don't think the board technically did anything wrong. The situation clearly became untennable which led to Jensen's willingness to resign today (no, I don't think he was *forced* to resign).

So refer back to the walls-closing-in analogy on the speed of his exit today -- that swiftness raises questions of more Conduct breaches over his 33 year tenure as CEO that may have come out in future.

Simple maths tells you that he likely left so quickly to preserve an ounce of dignity and to let Nvidia move forward which is somewhat admirable.

I’ve spent all day going back and forth on Nebius, asking myself whether I should trim some of my long shares or add more at these levels.

$CBRS had a killer earnings! Up 15% AH.

Cerebras just put up the kind of quarter that makes me look at the name differently.

Core revenue came in at $230.9M against ~$215M expected, up 70% from a year ago.

The real story is cloud. Cloud and services revenue grew 265% to $141.9M and is now about two-thirds of the business, while hardware sales fell 29%. Cerebras is turning into an inference cloud that also sells systems.

RPO sits at $26.1B, roughly 27x this year’s guided revenue already under contract.

They raised FY26 core revenue to $940M–$960M against $887M expected, and guided Q4 to $310M–$330M against $271M.

Q4 core gross margin is guided to 47%–49%, with core operating margin around breakeven. The losses are closing fast.

They have 700 MW of capacity under contract for delivery by the end of 2027, and the CEO said he expects revenue to triple next year.

GAAP is still messy. Revenue of $210.8M came in a hair light and EPS was −$0.67. The headlines will focus on that, but the backlog and the guide are what move this stock.

Inference is where AI spend is heading, and Cerebras was built for exactly that.

The stock is now down 70% after it's IPO, but we could be finally seeing it form a bottom.

Bullish!

One of my biggest lessons from 2026:

It's not just about how much you make during a rally. It's about how much you protect when the trend changes.

Semiconductors were responsible for a significant portion of my returns this year. But recognizing the warning signs and reducing exposure helped me protect roughly +60% YTD during this correction.

Throughout 2026, I've taken approximately 50 trades, averaging around 5 positions per month. Nearly 40% of those trades were in semiconductors and AI-related names.

That should tell you how heavily I participated in this sector and why recognizing the warning signs became so important.

Here's how it all played out.

1) The first warning sign came from $NVDA.

NVIDIA attempted a breakout but failed to sustain it. When one of the most important market leaders starts showing cracks, I pay attention.

2) The second warning was even more concerning.

Many semiconductor stocks were building the right side of their bases, looking like they were preparing for another leg higher.

Instead, we started seeing failed breakouts, sharp gap-downs, and deteriorating price action across the sector. That's when I started reducing my semiconductor exposure rather than buying dip.

Here are my semiconductor and AI infrastructure trades from 2026, including winners and losers:

$MRVL: +173% (final exit), +113% (first trim)
$ARM: +155% (final exit), +98% (first trim)
$MU: +146%
$NBIS: +60%
$TSEM: +33%
$TXN: +29%
$FPS: +25%
$ASX: +18%
$NVDA: +7%
$VICR: +4% and -9% (separate trades)
$KLAC: -9%
$STM: -9%
$CBRS: -9%
$P: -10%
$FORM: -34%
$VSH: -48%

Not every trade worked. I took losses, made mistakes, and certainly could have managed some positions better.

One exit I'm particularly happy with is $NBIS. I sold around $158 after it lost its 200-day SMA, locking in approximately 60% gains. Could I have sold into strength earlier? Absolutely, and that's one thing I could have done better.

So what's my plan now?

Over the past month, I haven't initiated any new semiconductor positions.

Instead, I've been focusing on hyperscalers like $MSFT and $META, along with $SPOT in digital streaming and $ISRG in healthcare and surgical robotics.

I'm looking for companies with strong fundamentals, constructive technical structures, and relative strength rather than forcing trades in a damaged sector.

And here's something I want to emphasize:

Many semiconductor leaders are technically broken charts. This is coming from someone who generated a significant portion of this year's returns from the sector.

I still believe many semiconductor companies have excellent long-term fundamentals. But strong fundamentals alone won't prevent a stock from entering a Stage 4 downtrend.

Many of these names need time to complete their Stage 4 declines, establish Stage 1 bases, and eventually transition back into Stage 2 uptrends.

That process could take weeks or months. Nobody knows exactly how long.There's no reason to stand in front of a moving train just because stocks are trading significantly below their highs.

Let the selling pressure ease, let the bases form, and let the technicals improve. We'll have opportunities again when the sector starts showing signs of accumulation.

My biggest takeaway:

You don't need to catch the exact bottom or sell at the exact top to make meaningful returns.

Follow the trend, respect the warning signs, manage your risk, and protect your capital when conditions deteriorate.

That's what Stage Analysis and disciplined position trading are all about.
Venu @Venu_7_ · 13 Oct 2026, 11:57 SGT
Sharing some of my thoughts on the recent weakness across AI and semiconductor names.

One thing I've always believed is that technicals often tell us about strength or weakness before the fundamentals and headlines catch up.

Looking at the broader semiconductor and memory theme, the recent price action is becoming concerning. I was expecting memory & semi stocks to build the right side of their bases, but looking back, the weakness we saw around June-July may have been an early warning sign.

We had a decent bounce over the last three months, but instead of building stronger bases, several names are now testing or losing their 50-day and 100-day moving averages.

On top of that, $NVDA is showing signs of a failed breakout, while $TSM, $SMTC, $NBIS and $LITE have also seen failed breakout attempts. Meanwhile, $AVGO has slipped below its 200-day SMA.

When stocks spend months consolidating, you want to see accumulation, higher lows, improving relative strength, and eventually a breakout. Instead, we're seeing failed breakout attempts, lower highs, and key moving averages being tested across multiple leaders in SemiConductor sector mainly.

One or two stocks showing weakness is normal, but when several leaders within the same theme start showing similar technical deterioration, that's something worth paying attention to.

A LOT of poor price action across semiconductor and AI names lately.

Does this mean the AI infrastructure cycle is over? Not at all! I still believe AI infrastructure has significant long-term growth potential.

But there's a difference between being bullish on a theme over the next 3-5 years and ignoring deteriorating price action in the short term.

As much as I'm bull at heart, you can't ignore what the market is telling you. Sometimes being patient and selective is just as important as being aggressive when the opportunities are there.

That being said, software, healthcare, crypto, and several other themes are holding up relatively well. Even some international markets, like Brazil, are showing encouraging signs of strength.

Just because one theme is correcting doesn't mean the entire market is falling apart. Capital can rotate from one area to another, and new market leaders can emerge while previous leaders consolidate.

The opportunities haven't disappeared. They're just not necessarily in the same places they were a few months ago!

The history books will be very kind to Jensen Huang.

Trillions in economic value created...all downstream from his visionary leadership decisions.

One decision was on CUDA.
Nvidia started funding it in ~2006 and kept funding it for years while it dragged margins. There was no AI market to justify the spend which led to huge skepticism on the Street.
His foresight will prove to be legendary.

The second was on Mellanox.
Paying $6.9B for a networking company in 2019 was viewed as a very odd move for Nvidia. In fact, I'd say that it's the deal that let Nvidia sell the whole rack instead of the chip which is where much of Nvidia's pricing power comes from today. Very few CEOs get a call like that right.

Absolute legend.

The technology sector accounts for 44% of total US pension fund equity allocation, according to a Bloomberg analysis of more than 70 pension funds.

US pension funds are more exposed to technology stocks than ever.

$ABCL AbCellera CEO Carl Hansen made some very bullish comments at Stifel today on the commercial potential of ABCL635:

The TL;DR: “On all those dimensions, we think ABCL635 now looks much, much better. Coming into this, even with the TPP of equal efficacy and better safety, we thought it could be a blockbuster product. Now we think it's multiples of that.”

This company used to quote $2B in peak sales for ABCL635 during the early days years ago. Then within the past year or so it changed to “we believe there's about a $6 billion TAM in the U.S. for non-hormonal options for the treatment of hot flashes”. Well, what’s the new peak sales estimate assuming 635 is flat out better than any other non-hormonal option, along with directly competing with hormonal therapies? Hansen mentions a product like this could potentially command a premium price in the market.

And then on top of that, it’s now going to be tested for treating prostate and breast cancer patients who experience similar effects to VMS during their therapy. AND we have 992 going into clinical trials, for even better dosing convenience than the once-monthly for 635.

635 has turned out to be an even bigger deal than we initially thought. And people already came in with high expectations…

I cannot wait to watch the coming years unfold.

Cost effectiveness of AI is becoming a hot topic.

As AI adoption accelerates, the focus is increasingly shifting from simply building more powerful models to maximizing the value generated by every dollar spent.

Not every task requires the most expensive or advanced AI model.

In fact, the global AI inference software market is projected to grow from $21.1 billion in 2026 to $80.9 billion by 2033, representing +283% growth.

As companies deploy AI at scale, reducing costs without sacrificing performance will be increasingly important.

The next phase of AI is about efficiency, not just computing power.

"Big investors are buying the dip. Retail traders are not"

Last week the S&P 500 had its worst week since April 2025, and BofA’s client data shows exactly who bought it and who ran.

The big money bought. Institutions put in $6.1B, about $4B of it through ETFs, and hedge funds were net buyers for the first time in four weeks.

Retail sold, for the fourth week in a row. They dumped $3.4B of single stocks while still putting $1.4B into ETFs.

$5.3B went into equity ETFs, the 4th-biggest week in BofA’s data, mostly broad US large-cap funds. Tech got bought for the first time in four weeks, and industrials saw their 15th straight week of outflows.

Since the April 2025 tariff shock, retail has been the one catching the falling knife.

This time retail was selling, and Thursday’s crash started with retail buying puts.

So the people who usually panic are the ones who stepped in, and the people who usually step in are the ones who panicked.

I've been a net buyer from Thursday until Tuesday.

When smart money buys what retail is dumping, I pay attention.

Bullish ⚡️

George from 🕹prodmgmt.world@nurijanian
00:34 SGT quoteTech
what is product management, if we break it down to first principles

there is an organization that exists to create value for the market it serves.

to create real value for a market, someone has to figure out what that market needs and design something that solves that need.

the solution must be something the organization can actually build and sell.

it must not conflict with the current strategy. ideally, it should clearly fit the strategy, strengthen it, or even help shape and define the strategy.

- it’s not linear; you take quite a few shots. good stuff takes time.
- it’s heavy on execution and grind, but it also has to be creative and maintain trust.
- experience and product sense matter a lot.
- work used to be done by many people. now maybe not so much, but it still requires others. someone has to lead it.

this function is key in an org, and i still think 1 orchestrator is best here (human or AI, tbc)

otherwise each function pushes into its own corner, and you never reach the bare equilibrium you need to be successful. the product has the wrong components, or gets shipped too late.

(bad product management can happen too. one person, but the wrong one, and you get the same result.)

who should be doing this role?

technically, anyone... assuming they are high-agency, analytical, creative, clear thinker and communicator, low ego, high trust and integrity, work well with others, and ideally have lots of good ideas, experience and/or at least talk to customers all day.

which is probably why companies keep looking.

$ARM

It’s been a while since I’ve taken a closer look at $ARM, but there have been some really interesting developments cooking in the background.

This week Google announced its new TPU 8i Max, the latest in its line of custom AI chips. Like TPU 8t and TPU 8i before it, it runs on Google’s own Arm-based Axion CPUs as the host, so Google’s newest AI chips are all being built around Arm, something the market seems to have overlooked.

Every TPU needs a CPU next to it to feed it data and run the work around it, which means every TPU Google adds pulls more Arm in with it.

Axion also runs Google’s regular cloud servers at up to 2x better price-performance than comparable x86 machines, and AI agent sandboxes run about 30% cheaper on it.

Arm-based servers were already more than 45% of server revenue in Q1, according to IDC, and Arm expects to pass 60% share across the top U.S. clouds by the end of 2026.

Google’s new TPUs are getting all the headlines, but don’t think for a second they’ll rise on their own. Every TPU ships with a CPU, and it’s built on Arm.

Great news for Arm.

Bullish ⚡️

$CRWV $NBIS $IREN $NVDA

I went through CoreWeave’s Q3 report and call line by line, and it’s the strongest neocloud print I’ve seen this year.

Revenue grew 168% to $3.66B, ahead of estimates, and adjusted operating income hit $379M against guidance of $200M to $260M.

Full-year guidance went up to $13.0B–$13.3B, and CoreWeave expects to exit 2026 at a $20B–$21B revenue run rate.

Demand is 10x available capacity through 2027, and every bit of 2028 capacity offered so far is already sold.

Backlog hit $132.5B, up 138% in a year. The part due within 24 months more than doubled to ~$48B.

Prices went up ~25% in July and another 10% after. Short-term capacity now sells for $40M+ per MW a year, and older Ampere and Hopper GPUs repriced 30–50% higher.

The interest bill everyone is worried about went from 25x operating income in Q1 to 2.2x in Q3. Over 75% of capex through 2027 is backed by investment-grade and enterprise customers, and management expects contracted cash flow to repay the debt.

130,000 GPUs come off contract in 2027 and 170,000 more in 2028. Re-signed at today’s prices, that’s close to $10B of run-rate revenue with zero new capex.

You simply are not bullish enough on AI compute.

We shouldn’t really hike into December let alone 50 bps.

Oil just had its biggest weekly drop since 2020. Stocks just had their worst week since April 2025.

CPI, is a rearview mirror, Yes, October was hot: 0.4% headline, 0.3% core. But core is running around 2.7% a year, right around its 40-year average. One ugly print is one data point, and the Fed is supposed to wait for the trend.

You don't hike into a supply shock.

Higher rates don't pump a single extra barrel of oil. They just break whatever was already wobbling.

And where was all this urgency in 2021, when inflation hit 7% and the Fed spent most of the year calling it transitory?

A 50bp move is for emergencies. Nothing here is an emergency.

If it were up to me, they wouldn't hike at all in anticipation of what’s to come.

Make it make sense please, we need to accelerate not slow down this growth machine.

Our direct experience with Nvidia, never shared before:

22 months ago, we published the below analysis raising concerns that Nvidia's AI chips were potentially being routed to China through Singapore.

Less than 24 hours later, Nvidia's Head of PR contacted us, directly addressing our analysis. Their message to us is included below.

At the time, in the previous 3 quarters, $17.4 billion of Nvidia's revenue came from Singapore versus $11.6 billion from China.

Furthermore, at the time, the US had ~5,375 data centers, China had 448, and Singapore had just 99. The numbers just did not add up. You can read our full analysis below.

Nvidia's PR team sent us the following message:

"The revenue associated with Singapore does not indicate diversion to China. Our public filings report 'bill to' not 'ship to' locations of our customers. Many of our customers have business entities in Singapore and use those entities for products destined for the US and the West. We insist that our partners comply with all applicable laws, and if we receive any information to the contrary, act accordingly. Our last 10-Q noted: 'most shipments associated with Singapore revenue were to locations other than Singapore and shipments to Singapore were insignificant.'"

Fast forward to today.

According to new reports, Nvidia, $NVDA, CEO Jensen Huang's relationship with a suspected Chinese spy helped facilitate at least $7.5 billion in Nvidia chip shipments to Chinese companies through a network spanning China and Singapore.

The reported shipments date back to 2023 and involved ~240,000 advanced Nvidia AI chips.

These allegations remain under investigation, and it is not yet established whether the shipments were connected to the revenue discrepancies we highlighted 22 months ago.

Nvidia maintains that it has no reason to believe US national security or company secrets were compromised.

But the overlap between these new allegations and the questions we raised in January 2025, along with Nvidia's response to us at the time, is noteworthy.

We stand by our view that Jensen Huang is likely to remain CEO of Nvidia and will continue to be an integral figure in the AI Revolution.

We expect more on this soon.

On the Nvidia situation:

Nvidia, $NVDA, is now down another -7% today and -12% since the Jensen Huang affair situation began.

At this point, the market is pricing in two major potential headwinds.

First, the growing possibility that Jensen Huang will be removed as CEO.

Second, possibility that sensitive Nvidia technology or information was compromised.

Are these scenarios possible? Sure, but we believe both remain unlikely, with less than a 20% probability.

Nvidia's stock is now down -32% in just 24 trading days, erasing -$1.8 trillion in market cap, with over one-third of these losses coinciding with the Jensen Huang controversy.

We believe Huang remains an integral part of Nvidia's future and the broader AI Revolution, and this week's events will not derail the broader thesis.

As the dust settles and uncertainty begins to fade, we expect bargain hunters to step in.

The fundamental AI investment thesis remains intact.

Why Nvidia is continuing to take a further hit today...

- The Information reported that a network linked to Alice Huang allegedly facilitated at least $7.5 billion in Nvidia chip shipments to Chinese companies, involving roughly 240,000 AI chips, including models restricted from sale in China. - Bloomberg reported that Nvidia's inventory figures provided to U.S. authorities undercounted approximately 50,000 AI chips worth billions of dollars sold to Megaspeed through hardware partners. Nvidia later claimed the hardware was located at additional warehouses but did not provide a detailed accounting. Basically, if those 50K chips aren't accounted for...could they have gone to China?

Both those headlines broke over the past 24 hours as Nvidia is now at a $4.02T marketcap, losing over $1T in value over the past month.
